Front: Respiration
Back: The process cells use to release energy from food. Oxygen and glucose are used; carbon dioxide and water are made.
Extra cue: Do not confuse with breathing. Breathing gets oxygen in; respiration releases energy in cells.

Front: Gas exchange
Back: The swap of gases in the lungs: oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out of the blood.
Extra cue: Happens in the lungs, then blood carries gases around the body.

Front: Breathing
Back: The muscle movement that makes the lungs expand and contract.
Extra cue: Breathing is the movement; ventilation is the movement of air.

Front: Ventilation
Back: Air moving into and out of the lungs.
Extra cue: Inhalation + exhalation together.

Front: Inhalation
Back: Breathing in.
Extra cue: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; rib muscles help increase chest volume.

Front: Exhalation
Back: Breathing out.
Extra cue: Chest volume decreases; air is forced out.

Front: Diaphragm
Back: A sheet of muscle below the lungs that helps change the volume of the chest.
Extra cue: Contracts and moves down during inhalation.

Front: Intercostal muscles
Back: Muscles between the ribs that move the rib cage during breathing.
Extra cue: Used with the diaphragm.

Front: Oxygen
Back: Gas needed for respiration.
Extra cue: Carried mainly by red blood cells.

Front: Carbon dioxide
Back: Waste gas made by respiration.
Extra cue: Removed from blood at the lungs and exhaled.

Front: Circulatory system
Back: The heart, blood and blood vessels that transport materials around the body.
Extra cue: Carries oxygen, nutrients and waste products.

Front: Heart
Back: The organ that pumps blood around the body.
Extra cue: Pulse is caused by the heart pumping blood into arteries.

Front: Artery
Back: Blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
Extra cue: Usually has thick walls and a pulse.

Front: Vein
Back: Blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart.
Extra cue: Returns blood to the heart.

Front: Capillary
Back: Tiny, thin-walled blood vessel where substances move between blood and body cells.
Extra cue: Thin walls help exchange oxygen, nutrients and carbon dioxide.

Front: Plasma
Back: Liquid part of the blood.
Extra cue: Carries dissolved nutrients and other substances.

Front: Red blood cell
Back: Blood cell that carries oxygen using haemoglobin.
Extra cue: Adapted by having large surface area and no nucleus.

Front: White blood cell
Back: Blood cell that helps fight micro-organisms.
Extra cue: Part of body defence.

Front: Bone marrow
Back: Tissue inside some bones where blood cells are made.
Extra cue: Links skeleton to blood production.

Front: Skeleton
Back: The framework of bones that supports and protects the body and helps movement.
Extra cue: Functions: support, protection, movement.

Front: Skull
Back: Bones that protect the brain.
Extra cue: Example of protection by skeleton.

Front: Ribs/sternum
Back: Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Extra cue: Another protection example.

Front: Vertebrae/backbone
Back: Small bones forming the spine.
Extra cue: Support the body and protect the spinal cord.

Front: Joint
Back: Place where two or more bones meet.
Extra cue: Can be fixed or flexible.

Front: Fixed joint
Back: Joint where bones meet but do not move much.
Extra cue: Example: skull joints.

Front: Flexible joint
Back: Joint that can be moved by muscles.
Extra cue: Example: elbow.

Front: Hinge joint
Back: Joint that allows back-and-forth movement in one direction.
Extra cue: Example: elbow/knee.

Front: Cartilage
Back: Smooth, slippery tissue at bone ends that reduces rubbing.
Extra cue: Helps joints move smoothly.

Front: Ligament
Back: Tissue that connects bone to bone.
Extra cue: Different from tendon.

Front: Tendon
Back: Tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Extra cue: Allows muscle pull to move bone.

Front: Muscle
Back: Tissue/organ that can contract and relax to create movement.
Extra cue: Muscles pull; they do not push.

Front: Contract
Back: Get shorter and thicker.
Extra cue: Contracting muscles pull bones.

Front: Relax
Back: Stop pulling strongly; can be stretched longer by the opposite muscle or load.
Extra cue: Muscles pull; they do not actively push themselves longer.

Front: Antagonistic pair
Back: Two muscles that move a bone in opposite directions.
Extra cue: One contracts while the other relaxes.

Front: Biceps and triceps
Back: Arm muscle pair that bends and straightens the elbow.
Extra cue: Biceps contracts to bend; triceps contracts to straighten.

Front: Impulse
Back: Electrical signal in the nervous system.
Extra cue: Carries messages from brain/spinal cord to muscles.

Front: Nervous system
Back: Brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Extra cue: Controls muscle action and reaction time.

Front: Drug
Back: Substance that affects how the body works.
Extra cue: Medicines are useful drugs; recreational drugs can be harmful.

Front: Stimulant
Back: Drug that speeds up nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Example: caffeine.

Front: Depressant
Back: Drug that slows down nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Example: alcohol.

Front: Reaction time
Back: Time taken to respond to something.
Extra cue: Can be changed by drugs.

Front: Side-effect
Back: Unwanted or harmful effect of a drug.
Extra cue: Important in drug safety/testing.

Front: Respiration word equation
Back: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy released
Extra cue: This is the main biology equation to memorise. It happens in cells, not just in the lungs.

Front: Breathing rate
Back: breathing rate = number of breaths per minute
Extra cue: Count one inhale + one exhale as one breath.

Front: Pulse rate
Back: pulse rate = number of heart beats per minute
Extra cue: Measured where an artery is close to the skin, such as the wrist or neck.

Front: Gas exchange direction
Back: oxygen: air in lungs -> blood; carbon dioxide: blood -> air in lungs
Extra cue: Use arrows to describe movement clearly.

Front: Pressure relationship
Back: pressure = force / area
Extra cue: Useful extension from the skeleton topic: the same force over a smaller area gives greater pressure.

Front: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
Back: Breathing moves air in/out of the lungs; respiration releases energy in cells.

Front: Why do muscles need oxygen and nutrients?
Back: For respiration, which releases energy for muscle contraction.

Front: Why are antagonistic pairs needed?
Back: A muscle can pull but cannot push, so another muscle is needed to pull the bone back.

Front: What do red blood cells, white blood cells and plasma do?
Back: Red blood cells carry oxygen; white blood cells fight micro-organisms; plasma carries dissolved substances.

Front: Hazard
Back: Something that could cause harm.
Extra cue: Example: corrosive acid.

Front: Risk
Back: The chance that a hazard will actually cause harm.
Extra cue: Risk can be lowered with precautions.

Front: Precaution
Back: Action taken to reduce risk.
Extra cue: Example: wear eye protection.

Front: Corrosive
Back: Able to damage or destroy materials and living tissue.
Extra cue: Most concentrated acids can be corrosive.

Front: Irritant
Back: Causes soreness or stinging, especially to skin or eyes.
Extra cue: Many dilute acids are irritants.

Front: Toxic
Back: Poisonous.
Extra cue: Avoid contact and ingestion.

Front: Flammable
Back: Catches fire easily.
Extra cue: Keep away from flames.

Front: Explosive
Back: Reacts very quickly, releasing energy, gas and sound.
Extra cue: Can be triggered by heat.

Front: Acid
Back: Solution with pH less than 7; turns blue litmus red.
Extra cue: Lower pH means more acidic.

Front: Alkali
Back: Solution with pH more than 7; turns red litmus blue.
Extra cue: Higher pH means more alkaline.

Front: Base
Back: Substance that neutralises an acid to form salt and water.
Extra cue: Can be soluble or insoluble. A soluble base is an alkali.

Front: Soluble
Back: Able to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Soluble base = alkali.

Front: Insoluble
Back: Unable to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Some bases are insoluble.

Front: Concentrated
Back: Contains a large amount of dissolved substance in a small amount of solvent.
Extra cue: More concentrated usually means more hazardous.

Front: Dilute/diluted
Back: Made less concentrated by adding water.
Extra cue: Dilute acids are less hazardous than concentrated acids.

Front: Indicator
Back: Dye that changes colour in acids and alkalis.
Extra cue: Used to test unknown solutions.

Front: Litmus
Back: Indicator: red in acid, blue in alkali.
Extra cue: Neutral keeps red litmus red and blue litmus blue.

Front: Universal indicator
Back: Indicator that shows a range of colours for different pH values.
Extra cue: Used to estimate pH.

Front: pH scale
Back: Scale from 1 to 14 showing acidity/alkalinity.
Extra cue: Acid < 7; neutral = 7; alkali > 7.

Front: Neutral
Back: Neither acid nor alkali; pH 7.
Extra cue: Pure water is neutral.

Front: Chemical reaction
Back: Change where new substances are formed.
Extra cue: Reactants become products.

Front: Reactants
Back: Starting substances in a reaction.
Extra cue: Written on the left of a word equation.

Front: Products
Back: New substances made in a reaction.
Extra cue: Written on the right of a word equation.

Front: Word equation
Back: Equation using names of substances with an arrow from reactants to products.
Extra cue: Arrow means react to form.

Front: Neutralisation
Back: Reaction where an acid reacts with an alkali/base to make salt and water only.
Extra cue: Core chemistry reaction for this unit.

Front: Salt
Back: Substance made, besides water, when an acid is neutralised by a base/alkali.
Extra cue: Salt name depends on acid and metal/base used.

Front: Antacid
Back: Medicine containing a base that neutralises excess stomach acid.
Extra cue: Everyday neutralisation example.

Front: Acid rain
Back: Rainwater made more acidic by air pollution.
Extra cue: Can damage plants, water systems and buildings.

Front: Neutralisation with alkali
Back: acid + alkali -> salt + water
Extra cue: Learn this exactly.

Front: Neutralisation with base
Back: acid + base -> salt + water
Extra cue: A base may be soluble or insoluble.

Front: Hydrochloric acid salt rule
Back: hydrochloric acid -> chloride salts
Extra cue: Example: zinc oxide + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + water.

Front: Nitric acid salt rule
Back: nitric acid -> nitrate salts
Extra cue: Example: magnesium oxide + nitric acid -> magnesium nitrate + water.

Front: Sulfuric acid salt rule
Back: sulfuric acid -> sulfate salts
Extra cue: Example: copper oxide + sulfuric acid -> copper sulfate + water.

Front: pH classification
Back: acid: pH < 7; neutral: pH = 7; alkali: pH > 7
Extra cue: The lower the acid pH, the more acidic. The higher the alkali pH, the more alkaline.

Front: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
Back: A hazard can cause harm; a risk is the chance it actually causes harm.

Front: What colour is litmus in acid and alkali?
Back: Acid: red. Alkali: blue.

Front: What are the products of neutralisation?
Back: A salt and water.

Front: How do you decide the second part of a salt name?
Back: It comes from the acid: hydrochloric gives chloride, nitric gives nitrate, sulfuric gives sulfate.

Front: Electricity
Back: A way of transferring energy through wires by moving charges.
Extra cue: Needs a complete circuit and a source such as a cell.

Front: Charge
Back: Tiny charged particles, such as electrons, can move around a circuit.
Extra cue: The flow of charged particles is current.

Front: Current
Back: Flow of electricity/charges around a circuit.
Extra cue: Measured in amps with an ammeter.

Front: Ampere / amp (A)
Back: Unit of current.
Extra cue: Symbol A.

Front: Ammeter
Back: Instrument that measures current.
Extra cue: Connect in series.

Front: Voltage
Back: Measure of energy transferred by electricity; the push from the source.
Extra cue: Measured in volts with a voltmeter.

Front: Volt (V)
Back: Unit of voltage.
Extra cue: Symbol V.

Front: Voltmeter
Back: Instrument that measures voltage.
Extra cue: Connect in parallel across a component.

Front: Cell
Back: Source of electrical energy in a circuit.
Extra cue: Cells push charges around a circuit.

Front: Power pack
Back: School-safe low-voltage supply.
Extra cue: Acts as a source of voltage.

Front: Component
Back: Part of a circuit, such as a bulb, switch, resistor or motor.
Extra cue: Use correct circuit symbols.

Front: Switch
Back: Component that opens or closes a circuit.
Extra cue: Open switch = gap = no current.

Front: Bulb
Back: Component that transfers electrical energy to light and heat.
Extra cue: Brightness can change with current/voltage and circuit layout.

Front: Filament
Back: Thin wire in a bulb that glows when current flows.
Extra cue: Transfers energy as light and heat.

Front: Conductor
Back: Material that allows electricity to flow through it.
Extra cue: Metals are good conductors.

Front: Insulator
Back: Material that does not allow electricity to flow easily.
Extra cue: Plastic is a good insulator.

Front: Resistance
Back: How difficult it is for current to flow.
Extra cue: High resistance gives smaller current.

Front: Resistor
Back: Component that increases resistance and reduces current.
Extra cue: Used to control current.

Front: Variable resistor
Back: Resistor whose resistance can be changed.
Extra cue: Changing resistance changes current.

Front: Series circuit
Back: Circuit with one loop/path.
Extra cue: Same current everywhere; one break stops all components.

Front: Parallel circuit
Back: Circuit with branches.
Extra cue: Current splits at branches; components can work independently.

Front: AND circuit
Back: Two switches arranged so both must be closed for the component to turn on.
Extra cue: Like switches in series.

Front: OR circuit
Back: Two switches arranged so either switch can turn the component on.
Extra cue: Like switches in parallel.

Front: Static electricity
Back: Attraction or repulsion caused when materials rub and charges build up.
Extra cue: Different from current electricity in a circuit.

Front: Model
Back: A representation that helps explain something complicated.
Extra cue: Circuit models are useful but not perfect.

Front: Analogy
Back: Model that compares something hard to understand with something familiar.
Extra cue: Example: central heating model for circuits.

Front: Fuse
Back: Safety wire that melts if current is too high.
Extra cue: Protects against overheating/fire.

Front: Fuse rating
Back: Largest current a fuse can carry without melting.
Extra cue: Use the correct fuse rating.

Front: Circuit breaker
Back: Safety device that switches off current if it gets too high.
Extra cue: Can be reset.

Front: Live wire
Back: Brown wire in a plug/cable; part of the circuit.
Extra cue: Dangerous if touched.

Front: Neutral wire
Back: Blue wire in a plug/cable; part of the circuit.
Extra cue: Completes the circuit.

Front: Earth wire
Back: Green/yellow safety wire.
Extra cue: Works with the fuse for safety.

Front: Ring main
Back: House wiring arrangement using a loop of parallel circuits.
Extra cue: Protected by circuit breakers.

Front: Current unit relationship
Back: current is measured in amperes (A)
Extra cue: Use an ammeter in series.

Front: Voltage unit relationship
Back: voltage is measured in volts (V)
Extra cue: Use a voltmeter in parallel.

Front: Series current rule
Back: I is the same everywhere in a series circuit
Extra cue: If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops.

Front: Parallel current rule
Back: I_total = I_branch 1 + I_branch 2 + ...
Extra cue: Current splits at branches and recombines later.

Front: Resistance-current relationship
Back: higher resistance -> lower current; lower resistance -> higher current
Extra cue: A resistor or thin wire increases resistance.

Front: Voltage-current relationship
Back: higher voltage -> higher current, if resistance stays the same
Extra cue: Biggest current: high voltage and low resistance.

Front: Optional extension: Ohm's law
Back: voltage = current x resistance, or V = I x R
Extra cue: Only use this if your teacher has taught it; it is a useful extension beyond the pack.

Front: Explain the different connection rules for an ammeter and a voltmeter.
Back: An ammeter is connected in series so the current flows through it. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component to compare the two sides.
Extra cue: This is one of the most common exam mistakes in circuits.

Front: Explain why adding more bulbs in series usually makes each bulb dimmer.
Back: Adding bulbs in series increases total resistance, so the current gets smaller. Smaller current means the bulbs are dimmer.
Extra cue: Do not say current is 'used up'; explain resistance and current.

Front: Explain why a bulb in another branch can stay on when one bulb breaks in a parallel circuit.
Back: Each branch has its own complete path. If one branch breaks, another branch can still be connected across the cell.
Extra cue: Parallel branches can work independently.

Front: Use the ideas of voltage and resistance to describe the circuit condition that gives the largest current.
Back: Largest current is produced by high voltage and low resistance, as long as the circuit is complete.
Extra cue: Open circuits still have zero current even if the voltage is high.

Front: Which statement best describes respiration?
Back: Cells release energy from glucose using oxygen.
Extra cue: Respiration happens in cells; breathing happens in the lungs.
Choices: Cells release energy from glucose using oxygen. | Air moves in and out of the lungs. | The heart pumps blood around the body. | Bones protect organs.

Front: What is the main job of red blood cells?
Back: Carry oxygen.
Extra cue: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
Choices: Carry oxygen. | Fight micro-organisms. | Make blood clot. | Digest food.

Front: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
Back: Artery.
Extra cue: Arteries go away from the heart.
Choices: Artery. | Vein. | Capillary. | Ligament.

Front: Where does gas exchange happen?
Back: In the lungs, where oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves blood.
Extra cue: Gas exchange is about oxygen and carbon dioxide moving between air and blood.
Choices: In the lungs, where oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves blood. | In the stomach, where food is broken down. | In bones, where blood cells are made. | In tendons, where muscles attach to bones.

Front: What happens to the diaphragm when you inhale?
Back: It contracts and moves down.
Extra cue: Moving down increases chest volume so air moves in.
Choices: It contracts and moves down. | It relaxes and moves up. | It turns oxygen into carbon dioxide. | It pumps blood to the lungs.

Front: What is ventilation?
Back: Air moving into and out of the lungs.
Extra cue: Ventilation is inhalation plus exhalation.
Choices: Air moving into and out of the lungs. | Energy release in cells. | Blood moving through arteries. | Muscles pulling on bones.

Front: Which part of the skeleton protects the brain?
Back: Skull.
Extra cue: The skull surrounds and protects the brain.
Choices: Skull. | Ribs. | Vertebrae. | Cartilage.

Front: Which bones help protect the heart and lungs?
Back: Ribs and sternum.
Extra cue: The rib cage protects organs in the chest.
Choices: Ribs and sternum. | Skull and jaw. | Femur and tibia. | Biceps and triceps.

Front: What is a joint?
Back: A place where two or more bones meet.
Extra cue: Joints can be fixed or movable.
Choices: A place where two or more bones meet. | A blood vessel where gas exchange happens. | A muscle that contracts. | A drug that slows nerve messages.

Front: What does cartilage do at the ends of bones?
Back: Reduces rubbing and helps bones move smoothly.
Extra cue: Cartilage is smooth and slippery.
Choices: Reduces rubbing and helps bones move smoothly. | Connects muscle to bone. | Carries oxygen. | Makes acid neutral.

Front: What connects bone to bone?
Back: Ligament.
Extra cue: Ligaments link bones at joints.
Choices: Ligament. | Tendon. | Capillary. | Plasma.

Front: What connects muscle to bone?
Back: Tendon.
Extra cue: Tendons transmit the pull from a muscle to a bone.
Choices: Tendon. | Ligament. | Artery. | Cartilage.

Front: Why are antagonistic muscle pairs needed?
Back: Muscles pull but cannot push, so another muscle pulls the bone back.
Extra cue: Biceps and triceps are a common example.
Choices: Muscles pull but cannot push, so another muscle pulls the bone back. | Bones can only move when they make blood cells. | Muscles only work when acid is neutralised. | Blood flows only in one direction through them.

Front: When the biceps contracts, what usually happens at the elbow?
Back: The arm bends.
Extra cue: The biceps pulls the forearm up.
Choices: The arm bends. | The arm straightens. | The ribs expand. | The skull moves.

Front: When the triceps contracts, what usually happens at the elbow?
Back: The arm straightens.
Extra cue: The triceps works opposite the biceps.
Choices: The arm straightens. | The arm bends. | The diaphragm moves down. | Blood becomes oxygen.

Front: What is the nervous system made from?
Back: Brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Extra cue: The nervous system sends impulses around the body.
Choices: Brain, spinal cord and nerves. | Heart, blood and blood vessels. | Bones, joints and cartilage. | Acids, alkalis and indicators.

Front: What is an impulse in the nervous system?
Back: An electrical signal.
Extra cue: Nerves carry electrical impulses.
Choices: An electrical signal. | A type of bone. | A waste gas. | A liquid part of blood.

Front: What is a stimulant?
Back: A drug that speeds up nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Caffeine is a common example of a stimulant.
Choices: A drug that speeds up nervous system messages. | A drug that slows nervous system messages. | A tissue connecting muscle to bone. | A solution with pH less than 7.

Front: What is a depressant?
Back: A drug that slows nervous system messages.
Extra cue: Depressants can slow reaction time.
Choices: A drug that slows nervous system messages. | A drug that speeds up nervous system messages. | A joint that moves in one direction. | A tiny blood vessel.

Front: What is reaction time?
Back: The time taken to respond to something.
Extra cue: A slower reaction time means a longer delay before responding.
Choices: The time taken to respond to something. | The amount of oxygen carried by blood. | The number of bones in the skeleton. | The pH of a solution.

Front: Which word equation is correct for respiration?
Back: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy released
Extra cue: This is the key life-process equation in the unit.
Choices: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy released | carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen | acid + alkali → salt + water | voltage = current × resistance

Front: What is pulse rate?
Back: Number of heart beats per minute.
Extra cue: Pulse tells you how often the heart is beating.
Choices: Number of heart beats per minute. | Number of breaths per minute. | Amount of oxygen per red blood cell. | Pressure divided by area.

Front: What does plasma do in blood?
Back: Carries dissolved substances.
Extra cue: Plasma is the liquid part of blood.
Choices: Carries dissolved substances. | Carries bones around the body. | Connects muscle to bone. | Turns blue litmus red.

Front: Why do muscles need oxygen and nutrients?
Back: For respiration to release energy for contraction.
Extra cue: Muscle contraction needs energy from respiration.
Choices: For respiration to release energy for contraction. | To make indicators change colour. | To increase the resistance of wires. | To turn arteries into veins.

Front: What is a hazard?
Back: Something that could cause harm.
Extra cue: Hazard = possible source of harm.
Choices: Something that could cause harm. | The chance harm will happen. | A solution with pH 7. | A salt made by neutralisation.

Front: What is risk?
Back: The chance that a hazard will actually cause harm.
Extra cue: Risk can be reduced by precautions.
Choices: The chance that a hazard will actually cause harm. | Something that always causes harm. | A dye that changes colour. | A substance with pH more than 7.

Front: What does corrosive mean?
Back: Can damage or destroy materials and living tissue.
Extra cue: Corrosive chemicals need careful handling.
Choices: Can damage or destroy materials and living tissue. | Catches fire easily. | Cannot dissolve in water. | Shows pH using colours.

Front: What does flammable mean?
Back: Catches fire easily.
Extra cue: Flammable substances need to be kept away from flames.
Choices: Catches fire easily. | Poisonous. | Damages tissue. | Neither acid nor alkali.

Front: What is an acid?
Back: A solution with pH less than 7.
Extra cue: Acids turn blue litmus red.
Choices: A solution with pH less than 7. | A solution with pH more than 7. | A neutral solution only. | A substance that cannot dissolve.

Front: What is an alkali?
Back: A solution with pH more than 7.
Extra cue: Alkalis turn red litmus blue.
Choices: A solution with pH more than 7. | A solution with pH less than 7. | A substance that always catches fire. | A tiny blood vessel.

Front: What pH is neutral?
Back: pH 7.
Extra cue: Water is often used as the simple neutral example.
Choices: pH 7. | pH 1. | pH 14. | Any pH below 7.

Front: What colour does blue litmus turn in acid?
Back: Red.
Extra cue: Acid turns blue litmus red.
Choices: Red. | Blue. | Green. | Purple.

Front: What colour does red litmus turn in alkali?
Back: Blue.
Extra cue: Alkali turns red litmus blue.
Choices: Blue. | Red. | Orange. | Yellow.

Front: What is universal indicator used for?
Back: Showing a range of pH values using different colours.
Extra cue: Universal indicator gives more information than litmus.
Choices: Showing a range of pH values using different colours. | Measuring current in a circuit. | Connecting muscle to bone. | Making a circuit safer.

Front: What is neutralisation?
Back: An acid reacts with an alkali or base to make salt and water.
Extra cue: Neutralisation is a chemical reaction.
Choices: An acid reacts with an alkali or base to make salt and water. | A wire melts when current is too high. | Air moves into and out of the lungs. | A muscle gets shorter and thicker.

Front: What are the products of acid + alkali?
Back: Salt and water.
Extra cue: The standard equation is acid + alkali → salt + water.
Choices: Salt and water. | Glucose and oxygen. | Carbon dioxide and energy. | Current and voltage.

Front: What is a base?
Back: A substance that neutralises an acid to form salt and water.
Extra cue: An alkali is a soluble base.
Choices: A substance that neutralises an acid to form salt and water. | A gas needed for respiration. | A circuit with one loop. | A blood vessel that carries blood away.

Front: What does soluble mean?
Back: Able to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Soluble substances dissolve.
Choices: Able to dissolve in a liquid. | Unable to dissolve in a liquid. | Can destroy living tissue. | Has a pH less than 7.

Front: What does insoluble mean?
Back: Unable to dissolve in a liquid.
Extra cue: Insoluble substances do not dissolve.
Choices: Unable to dissolve in a liquid. | Able to dissolve in a liquid. | Made less concentrated by water. | Turns red litmus blue.

Front: What does dilute mean?
Back: Made less concentrated by adding water.
Extra cue: Diluting reduces concentration.
Choices: Made less concentrated by adding water. | Contains a lot of solute in a small solvent volume. | Cannot dissolve. | Catches fire easily.

Front: What does concentrated mean?
Back: Contains a large amount of dissolved substance in a small amount of solvent.
Extra cue: Concentrated is not the same as strong acid at this level.
Choices: Contains a large amount of dissolved substance in a small amount of solvent. | Made less concentrated by adding water. | Neither acid nor alkali. | A dye that always stays the same colour.

Front: What are reactants?
Back: Starting substances in a chemical reaction.
Extra cue: Reactants are written before the arrow in a word equation.
Choices: Starting substances in a chemical reaction. | New substances made by a reaction. | Tiny moving charges. | The liquid part of blood.

Front: What are products?
Back: New substances made in a chemical reaction.
Extra cue: Products are written after the arrow in a word equation.
Choices: New substances made in a chemical reaction. | Starting substances in a reaction. | Materials that let current flow. | Bones that protect the brain.

Front: What does hydrochloric acid make in salt names?
Back: Chloride salts.
Extra cue: The acid gives the second part of the salt name.
Choices: Chloride salts. | Nitrate salts. | Sulfate salts. | Carbonate salts.

Front: What does nitric acid make in salt names?
Back: Nitrate salts.
Extra cue: Nitric acid gives nitrate.
Choices: Nitrate salts. | Chloride salts. | Sulfate salts. | Oxide salts.

Front: What does sulfuric acid make in salt names?
Back: Sulfate salts.
Extra cue: Sulfuric acid gives sulfate.
Choices: Sulfate salts. | Chloride salts. | Nitrate salts. | Hydroxide salts.

Front: Why can antacids help indigestion?
Back: They contain bases that neutralise excess stomach acid.
Extra cue: Antacid means anti-acid.
Choices: They contain bases that neutralise excess stomach acid. | They increase the acidity of the stomach. | They carry oxygen to muscles. | They reduce resistance in wires.

Front: What is acid rain?
Back: Rainwater made more acidic by air pollution.
Extra cue: Acid rain can damage materials and living things.
Choices: Rainwater made more acidic by air pollution. | Rainwater with pH exactly 7. | Water made more alkaline by salt. | Rain that carries red blood cells.

Front: A lamp is lit in a complete circuit. Which statement best describes the current in the wires?
Back: Charges flow around the complete circuit.
Extra cue: Current is the flow of charge; it is not the same as voltage or energy stored in the cell.
Choices: Charges flow around the complete circuit.|Voltage is used up by the first bulb.|Resistance flows from the cell.|Only energy, not charges, moves through the wires.

Front: An ammeter reading is written as 0.35 __. Which unit completes the reading?
Back: A
Extra cue: Current is measured in amperes, written as A.
Choices: A|V|Ω|J

Front: A student wants to measure the current through a bulb. Where should the ammeter be connected?
Back: In series with the bulb, so the same current passes through the ammeter and the bulb.
Extra cue: Ammeters are placed in the main path of the current.
Choices: In series with the bulb, so the same current passes through the ammeter and the bulb.|In parallel across the bulb, so it measures the energy transferred.|Across the cell only, because all current starts at the cell.|Next to the circuit but not connected, because it senses current.

Front: A cell has a larger voltage than another cell. What does that mean for the charges in the circuit?
Back: More energy is transferred to the charges by the cell.
Extra cue: Voltage is a measure of energy transferred per charge; at this level it is often described as electrical 'push'.
Choices: More energy is transferred to the charges by the cell.|The current must be smaller everywhere.|The wires become better insulators.|The circuit automatically becomes parallel.

Front: A student wants to measure the voltage across a lamp. Where should the voltmeter be connected?
Back: In parallel across the lamp.
Extra cue: Voltmeters compare the two sides of a component, so they connect across it.
Choices: In parallel across the lamp.|In series before the lamp.|In series after the lamp.|In place of the cell.

Front: A simple circuit has a cell, wires and a bulb. What is the main role of the cell?
Back: It transfers energy to the charges and pushes them around the circuit.
Extra cue: A cell is a source of electrical energy.
Choices: It transfers energy to the charges and pushes them around the circuit.|It measures how much current is flowing.|It increases resistance so no current flows.|It turns the wires into insulators.

Front: A switch is open in a simple lamp circuit. Which explanation is correct?
Back: There is a gap in the circuit, so current cannot flow through the lamp.
Extra cue: Open switch = gap; closed switch = complete path.
Choices: There is a gap in the circuit, so current cannot flow through the lamp.|The cell has no voltage until the switch is removed.|The current flows only through the air gap.|The bulb is brighter because resistance is lower.

Front: Which material would be most suitable for the wires in a school circuit?
Back: A metal, because it allows electric charge to flow easily.
Extra cue: Metals are good electrical conductors.
Choices: A metal, because it allows electric charge to flow easily.|Plastic, because it lets current pass with no resistance.|Rubber, because it stores current safely.|Wood, because it gives charges more energy.

Front: Why is the outside of many electrical cables made from plastic?
Back: Plastic is an insulator, so it reduces the chance of current passing through a person touching it.
Extra cue: Insulators are useful for safety because they do not allow charge to flow easily.
Choices: Plastic is an insulator, so it reduces the chance of current passing through a person touching it.|Plastic is a conductor, so it carries current faster than metal.|Plastic increases voltage so the circuit works better.|Plastic makes the circuit parallel.

Front: A wire has high resistance. What does this tell you about current in that wire?
Back: It is more difficult for current to flow through the wire.
Extra cue: Higher resistance usually means smaller current for the same voltage.
Choices: It is more difficult for current to flow through the wire.|Charges have more paths to choose from.|The voltage is always zero.|The wire must be a voltmeter.

Front: A resistor is added in series with a lamp. What is the most likely effect?
Back: The current is reduced, so the lamp may become dimmer.
Extra cue: More resistance makes current smaller if voltage stays the same.
Choices: The current is reduced, so the lamp may become dimmer.|The current increases because there is another component.|The resistor stores all the current permanently.|The circuit turns from series into parallel.

Front: A dimmer control changes the brightness of a lamp by changing resistance. Which component could do this?
Back: A variable resistor.
Extra cue: Variable resistors can change the size of the current.
Choices: A variable resistor.|A fixed cell.|A closed switch only.|An ammeter in parallel.

Front: Which description identifies a series circuit?
Back: There is one loop, so all components are on the same current path.
Extra cue: Series circuits do not have separate branches.
Choices: There is one loop, so all components are on the same current path.|There are separate branches for each component.|The circuit must contain a voltmeter.|Each component has its own cell.

Front: Which description identifies a parallel circuit?
Back: The circuit splits into branches and then joins again.
Extra cue: Parallel circuits have more than one path for current.
Choices: The circuit splits into branches and then joins again.|All components are placed on one loop only.|There is no complete path for current.|The circuit contains no switches.

Front: Two ammeters are placed at different points in one series loop. What should their readings show?
Back: The same current at both points.
Extra cue: Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
Choices: The same current at both points.|Less current after each bulb.|More current after each bulb.|Zero current near the cell.

Front: A parallel circuit has two branches. The branch currents are 0.2 A and 0.3 A. What is the total current from the cell?
Extra cue: In a parallel circuit, total current equals the sum of the branch currents.

Front: One bulb breaks in one branch of a parallel circuit. What usually happens to a bulb in another complete branch?
Back: It can stay lit because its branch is still complete.
Extra cue: Branches can work independently if their paths remain complete.
Choices: It can stay lit because its branch is still complete.|It must go out because current is used up.|It becomes a cell for the broken branch.|It makes the other branch series.

Front: A second identical bulb is added in series with the first bulb. What usually happens to the brightness?
Back: Both bulbs are dimmer because total resistance increases and current decreases.
Extra cue: More components in one path usually means more resistance.
Choices: Both bulbs are dimmer because total resistance increases and current decreases.|Both bulbs are brighter because the voltage is doubled.|Only the first bulb lights because it uses all the current.|The second bulb lights but the first one becomes a switch.

Front: Which circuit is likely to have the largest current?
Back: A high-voltage supply with a low-resistance path.
Extra cue: Current increases with voltage and decreases with resistance.
Choices: A high-voltage supply with a low-resistance path.|A low-voltage supply with a high-resistance path.|An open switch with a low-resistance lamp.|No cell but very short wires.

Front: A resistor has current I through it and voltage V across it. Which equation links voltage, current and resistance?
Back: V = I × R
Extra cue: Ohm’s law can be rearranged to find current or resistance.
Choices: V = I × R|I = V × R|R = V × I|V = R ÷ I

Front: A lamp should turn on only when two separate switches are both closed. Which switch arrangement is needed?
Back: An AND circuit.
Extra cue: AND means switch A and switch B must both be closed.
Choices: An AND circuit.|An OR circuit.|A short circuit.|A voltmeter branch.

Front: A lamp should turn on when either of two switches is closed. Which switch arrangement is needed?
Back: An OR circuit.
Extra cue: OR means switch A or switch B can complete the path.
Choices: An OR circuit.|An AND circuit.|One open switch in series.|A resistor-only circuit.

Front: Too much current flows through a plug. What should the fuse do?
Back: Melt and break the circuit before the cable overheats.
Extra cue: A fuse is a safety device that breaks the circuit when current is too large.
Choices: Melt and break the circuit before the cable overheats.|Increase the current so the appliance works faster.|Measure the voltage across the appliance.|Turn the live wire into the neutral wire.

Front: In a UK-style plug, which wire is green and yellow and is included for safety?
Back: Earth wire.
Extra cue: Live is brown, neutral is blue, earth is green/yellow.
Choices: Earth wire.|Live wire.|Neutral wire.|Fuse wire.

Front: This symbol has one long line and one short line. What component does it represent?
Back: Cell
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Cell|Battery|Open switch|Resistor

Front: This symbol shows more than one cell joined together. What does it represent?
Back: Battery
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Battery|Single cell|Voltmeter|Closed switch

Front: This symbol has a circle with a cross inside it. What component does it represent?
Back: Lamp / bulb
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Lamp / bulb|Motor|Resistor|Ammeter

Front: This switch symbol shows a gap. What does it represent?
Back: Open switch
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Open switch|Closed switch|Cell|Fuse

Front: This switch symbol has no gap between the contacts. What does it represent?
Back: Closed switch
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Closed switch|Open switch|Voltmeter|Variable resistor

Front: This rectangular component symbol makes current more difficult to flow. What is it?
Back: Resistor
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Resistor|Lamp / bulb|Battery|Ammeter

Front: This meter has the letter A. How should this component be used?
Back: Ammeter
Extra cue: Ammeter measures current and is connected in series.
Choices: Ammeter|Voltmeter|Motor|Cell

Front: This meter has the letter V. What quantity does it measure?
Back: Voltmeter
Extra cue: Voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel.
Choices: Voltmeter|Ammeter|Battery|Switch

Front: This symbol has the letter M inside a circle. What component does it represent?
Back: Motor
Extra cue: Recognise the symbol and link it to the job of the component.
Choices: Motor|Lamp / bulb|Resistor|Voltmeter

Front: In this series circuit, bulb A breaks. Predict what happens to bulb B and explain why.
Back: Bulb B goes out because the single loop is broken and no current can flow anywhere in the circuit.
Extra cue: Series circuits have one path; one break stops the whole circuit.
Choices: Bulb B goes out because the single loop is broken and no current can flow anywhere in the circuit.|Bulb B stays on because it has its own branch.|Bulb B gets brighter because it receives more voltage.|Only bulb A goes out because current can go around it.

Front: In this parallel circuit, bulb A breaks. Predict what happens to bulb B and explain why.
Back: Bulb B can stay on because it is in a different complete branch.
Extra cue: Parallel circuits have separate paths for current.
Choices: Bulb B can stay on because it is in a different complete branch.|Bulb B must go out because current is used up in bulb A.|Bulb B gets no voltage because bulb A is broken.|The whole circuit becomes a series circuit.

Front: The ammeter labelled A is in the main loop. Why is this the correct position for measuring current?
Back: It is in series, so the same current that passes through the lamp also passes through the ammeter.
Extra cue: An ammeter must be part of the path whose current is being measured.
Choices: It is in series, so the same current that passes through the lamp also passes through the ammeter.|It is in parallel, so it measures voltage across the lamp.|It is across the cell, so it measures resistance.|It is outside the loop, so it does not affect the circuit.

Front: The voltmeter labelled A is connected across the lamp. Why is this the correct position?
Back: It is in parallel across the lamp, so it measures the voltage across that lamp.
Extra cue: A voltmeter compares two points, so it goes across the component.
Choices: It is in parallel across the lamp, so it measures the voltage across that lamp.|It is in series, so it measures current through the lamp.|It replaces the cell and supplies the voltage.|It increases the resistance so the lamp is safe.

Front: The diagram shows a voltmeter connected in the main loop. What is wrong, and how should it be connected?
Back: The voltmeter is connected in series; it should be connected in parallel across the component.
Extra cue: Voltmeters go across components, not in the main current path.
Choices: The voltmeter is connected in series; it should be connected in parallel across the component.|The lamp symbol is upside down; it should be replaced by a switch.|The cell has no voltage; it should be replaced by an ammeter.|The circuit is parallel; all voltmeters must be in series.

Front: In the AND switch circuit, switch A closes but switch B stays open. What happens?
Back: The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed to complete the circuit.
Extra cue: AND means A and B.
Choices: The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed to complete the circuit.|The lamp lights because one switch is closed.|The lamp lights because the switches are in parallel.|The lamp gets dimmer but stays on.

Front: In the OR switch circuit, switch A closes and switch B stays open. What happens?
Back: The lamp lights because either switch can complete a branch.
Extra cue: OR means A or B.
Choices: The lamp lights because either switch can complete a branch.|The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed.|The lamp stays off because switch B controls all branches.|The lamp lights only if both branches are broken.

Front: The switch labelled A is open. Explain why the lamp is not lit.
Back: The open switch leaves a gap, so the circuit is incomplete and current cannot flow.
Extra cue: Open switch = incomplete circuit.
Choices: The open switch leaves a gap, so the circuit is incomplete and current cannot flow.|The open switch lowers resistance to zero.|The cell has no energy when a switch is open.|The current jumps across the gap only at high voltage.

Front: The arrows labelled A show current direction. Which statement is the best interpretation?
Back: They show the direction of conventional current around the complete circuit.
Extra cue: At this level, arrows are often used to show conventional current direction.
Choices: They show the direction of conventional current around the complete circuit.|They show the direction in which voltage is used up.|They show resistance moving from the bulb to the cell.|They show charges leaving the circuit permanently.

Front: The diagram contains a short-circuit path. What is wrong with the connection?
Back: The extra wire bypasses the lamp, so most current takes the easier path instead of passing through the lamp.
Extra cue: Short circuits provide an unintended low-resistance path.
Choices: The extra wire bypasses the lamp, so most current takes the easier path instead of passing through the lamp.|The lamp is correctly placed in parallel with a switch.|The cell has been connected backwards.|The ammeter has been connected across the lamp.

Front: On the pH scale, which label shows an acid?
Back: A
Extra cue: Acids have pH values below 7.
Choices: A|B|C|None of them

Front: On the pH scale, which label is neutral?
Back: B
Extra cue: Pure water is about pH 7, which is neutral.
Choices: B|A|C|Both A and C

Front: On the pH scale, which label shows the most alkaline solution?
Back: C
Extra cue: The highest pH values are the most alkaline.
Choices: C|A|B|None of them

Front: What does blue litmus do in the acid beaker?
Back: Turns red.
Extra cue: Blue litmus turns red in acid.
Choices: Turns red.|Turns blue.|Turns green.|Makes a salt.

Front: What does red litmus do in the alkali beaker?
Back: Turns blue.
Extra cue: Red litmus turns blue in alkali.
Choices: Turns blue.|Turns red.|Turns white.|Measures current.

Front: In the universal indicator colours, which label is closest to neutral?
Back: B
Extra cue: Universal indicator is green near pH 7.
Choices: B|A|C|A and C

Front: In the universal indicator colours, which label is most acidic?
Back: A
Extra cue: Red/orange colours indicate acid.
Choices: A|B|C|None of them

Front: In the universal indicator colours, which label is most alkaline?
Back: C
Extra cue: Blue/purple colours indicate alkali.
Choices: C|A|B|All of them

Front: In the neutralisation setup, what is usually added to show the end point?
Back: Indicator.
Extra cue: Indicator changes colour when the acid has neutralised the alkali.
Choices: Indicator.|Ammeter.|Cartilage.|Red blood cells.

Front: In the neutralisation setup, what reaction is being tested?
Back: Acid + alkali → salt + water.
Extra cue: Neutralisation makes a salt and water.
Choices: Acid + alkali → salt + water.|Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.|Current = voltage ÷ resistance.|Bone + tendon → cartilage.

Front: What is the purpose of heating the solution in an evaporation dish?
Back: To evaporate water and leave salt crystals.
Extra cue: Evaporation removes the solvent.
Choices: To evaporate water and leave salt crystals.|To make current flow.|To make the pH always 14.|To contract the biceps.

Front: What is the main safety mistake in the diagram?
Back: Acid is being poured without clear eye protection.
Extra cue: Acid practicals need goggles and careful handling.
Choices: Acid is being poured without clear eye protection.|The beaker is made of glass.|The liquid is below pH 7.|The student is using indicator.

Front: What is wrong with this indicator method?
Back: Too much indicator has been added.
Extra cue: Usually only a few drops of indicator are needed.
Choices: Too much indicator has been added.|The beaker should be a battery.|Indicator should never change colour.|The acid has become a muscle.

Front: What is the safer way to dilute acid?
Back: Add acid slowly to water.
Extra cue: Use care: acid into water, slowly, with goggles.
Choices: Add acid slowly to water.|Add water quickly to concentrated acid.|Use no eye protection.|Heat it until it splashes.

Front: Why should you add alkali slowly during neutralisation?
Back: To avoid overshooting the neutral point.
Extra cue: Adding too much can make the solution alkaline instead of neutral.
Choices: To avoid overshooting the neutral point.|To make the bulb brighter.|To stop muscles contracting.|To make current flow backwards.

Front: A student says: “pH 1 is a strong alkali.” What is wrong?
Back: pH 1 is very acidic.
Extra cue: Low pH means acidic; high pH means alkaline.
Choices: pH 1 is very acidic.|pH 1 is neutral.|pH 1 is the strongest alkali.|pH only applies to electricity.

Front: In the elbow joint diagram, which label shows cartilage?
Back: A
Extra cue: Cartilage is smooth tissue at the ends of bones.
Choices: A|B|C|None of them

Front: In the elbow joint diagram, which label shows a ligament?
Back: B
Extra cue: Ligaments connect bone to bone.
Choices: B|A|C|All of them

Front: In the elbow joint diagram, which label shows a tendon?
Back: C
Extra cue: Tendons connect muscle to bone.
Choices: C|A|B|None of them

Front: In the arm diagram, which label is the biceps muscle?
Back: A
Extra cue: The biceps contracts to bend the elbow.
Choices: A|B|C|The diaphragm

Front: In the arm diagram, which label is the triceps muscle?
Back: B
Extra cue: The triceps contracts to straighten the elbow.
Choices: B|A|C|Cartilage

Front: In the arm diagram, why are A and B called an antagonistic pair?
Back: One contracts while the other relaxes to move the bone in opposite directions.
Extra cue: Muscles pull; they do not push.
Choices: One contracts while the other relaxes to move the bone in opposite directions.|They both push the bone together.|They are both acids.|They measure current.

Front: In the skeleton diagram, which label shows the skull?
Back: A
Extra cue: The skull protects the brain.
Choices: A|B|C|None of them

Front: In the skeleton diagram, which label shows the ribs?
Back: B
Extra cue: The ribs protect the heart and lungs.
Choices: B|A|C|All of them

Front: In the skeleton diagram, which label shows the backbone/spine area?
Back: C
Extra cue: The backbone supports the body and protects the spinal cord.
Choices: C|A|B|A bulb

Front: In the breathing diagram, which label shows the trachea/airway?
Back: A
Extra cue: Label A points to the trachea, the airway carrying air to and from the lungs.
Choices: A|B|C|D

Front: In the breathing diagram, which label shows a lung?
Back: B
Extra cue: Label B points to a lung.
Choices: B|A|C|D

Front: In the breathing diagram, which label shows the diaphragm?
Back: D
Extra cue: Label D points to the diaphragm, the muscle under the lungs.
Choices: D|A|B|C

Front: In the gas exchange diagram, which label shows oxygen moving into the blood?
Back: A
Extra cue: Oxygen moves from the air in the alveolus into the blood.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the gas exchange diagram, which label shows carbon dioxide moving into the air sac?
Back: B
Extra cue: Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air in the alveolus.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the blood-vessels diagram, which label shows the artery?
Back: A
Extra cue: The artery has the thickest wall and the smallest central space.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the blood-vessels diagram, which label shows the vein?
Back: B
Extra cue: The vein has a larger central space and a valve.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the blood-vessels diagram, which label shows capillaries?
Back: C
Extra cue: Capillaries are tiny, thin-walled vessels arranged in a network.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the ruler-drop test, what does the distance fallen help estimate?
Back: Reaction time.
Extra cue: The longer the ruler falls before being caught, the slower the reaction.
Choices: Reaction time.|pH value.|Voltage.|Bone strength.

Front: A student says: “Muscles push bones to move them.” What is wrong?
Back: Muscles pull when they contract; they do not push.
Extra cue: Movement usually needs antagonistic pairs.
Choices: Muscles pull when they contract; they do not push.|Muscles only work in acids.|Bones contract to pull muscles.|Tendons connect bone to bone.

Front: A student says: “Tendons connect bone to bone.” What is wrong?
Back: Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone.
Extra cue: This is a common exam mix-up.
Choices: Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone.|Tendons are pH indicators.|Ligaments connect muscles to batteries.|Cartilage carries oxygen.

Front: Trachea
Back: The tube that carries air from the mouth and nose down towards the lungs.
Extra cue: Also called the windpipe.

Front: Bronchi
Back: The two main tubes that carry air from the trachea into the lungs.
Extra cue: Each bronchus goes into one lung.

Front: Lungs
Back: Organs where gas exchange happens: oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves the blood.
Extra cue: The lungs are protected by the rib cage.

Front: Which organ is the main site of gas exchange?
Back: lungs
Extra cue: Gas exchange means oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves blood.
Choices: lungs|stomach|skull|femur

Front: What happens to oxygen during gas exchange in the lungs?
Back: Oxygen moves from the air spaces into the blood.
Extra cue: Oxygen is then carried to body cells for respiration.
Choices: Oxygen moves from the air spaces into the blood.|Oxygen is made by the ribs.|Oxygen turns into plasma.|Oxygen leaves the blood and enters the lungs.

Front: What happens to carbon dioxide during gas exchange in the lungs?
Back: Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air spaces in the lungs.
Extra cue: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration and is exhaled.
Choices: Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air spaces in the lungs.|Carbon dioxide moves from air into the blood.|Carbon dioxide becomes oxygen in the lungs.|Carbon dioxide is made by bones.

Front: Double circulatory system
Back: A circulation system with two loops: heart to lungs to heart, and heart to body to heart.
Extra cue: Blood passes through the heart twice for each full circuit of the body.

Front: What are the two loops in the human double circulatory system?
Back: Heart → lungs → heart, and heart → body → heart.
Extra cue: The lung loop picks up oxygen; the body loop delivers oxygen to cells.

Front: Why does blood go to the lungs in one loop of double circulation?
Back: To pick up oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide.
Extra cue: Then oxygen-rich blood returns to the heart before being pumped to the body.
Choices: To pick up oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide.|To make bones harder.|To digest food.|To change red blood cells into white blood cells.

Front: What happens to the chambers of the heart when heart muscle contracts?
Back: The chambers get smaller and force blood out.
Extra cue: This pumping can be felt as a pulse in arteries.
Choices: The chambers get smaller and force blood out.|The chambers fill with air.|The chambers turn into capillaries.|The chambers stop blood moving.

Front: Artery adaptation
Back: Arteries have thick, strong walls to carry blood away from the heart under pressure.
Extra cue: A pulse can be felt in arteries.

Front: Vein adaptation
Back: Veins carry blood back to the heart and have thinner walls than arteries.
Extra cue: At this level, remember: arteries away, veins back.

Front: Capillary adaptation
Back: Capillaries are tiny blood vessels with very thin walls, often one cell thick, for exchange with tissues.
Extra cue: Thin walls let oxygen and nutrients leave the blood easily.

Front: Which blood vessel has walls one cell thick for exchange?
Back: capillary
Extra cue: Capillaries link arteries and veins and allow substances to move in and out of blood.
Choices: capillary|artery|vein|tendon

Front: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Back: arteries
Extra cue: Artery starts with A: away from the heart.
Choices: arteries|veins|capillaries|ligaments

Front: Which blood vessels carry blood back to the heart?
Back: veins
Extra cue: Veins return blood to the heart.
Choices: veins|arteries|capillaries|tendons

Front: Newton
Back: The unit used to measure force; symbol N.
Extra cue: Example: a force of 10 N.

Front: What unit is force measured in?
Back: newtons
Extra cue: The symbol for newtons is N.
Choices: newtons|amps|volts|pH

Front: Quadriceps
Back: A group of muscles at the front of the thigh that can help straighten the leg.
Extra cue: Like biceps/triceps, leg muscles work in antagonistic pairs.

Front: Why do muscles need to work in pairs?
Back: Muscles can pull but cannot push.
Extra cue: One muscle contracts while the other relaxes.
Choices: Muscles can pull but cannot push.|Muscles can only push.|Bones contract by themselves.|Tendons make oxygen.

Front: Scientific question
Back: A question that can be answered using evidence from observations or experiments.
Extra cue: Example: Does caffeine affect reaction time?

Front: Non-scientific question
Back: A question that cannot be answered by a science experiment or measurement.
Extra cue: Example: Which sport is the most fun?

Front: Ethical question
Back: A question about what people think is fair, right, or wrong.
Extra cue: Example: Is it right to test a medicine on animals?

Front: Which is a scientific question?
Back: Does exercise change pulse rate?
Extra cue: It can be tested by measuring pulse before and after exercise.
Choices: Does exercise change pulse rate?|Is running the best sport?|Should everyone have to exercise?|Is it fair to ban fizzy drinks?

Front: Which is an ethical question?
Back: Is it fair to test a new drug on animals?
Extra cue: Ethical questions are about right/wrong and fairness.
Choices: Is it fair to test a new drug on animals?|What is pulse rate measured in?|Does caffeine affect reaction time?|How many bones are in the arm?

Front: Medicine
Back: A drug used to help prevent or treat disease or pain.
Extra cue: Examples include paracetamol and antibiotics such as penicillin.

Front: Recreational drug
Back: A drug taken because people like its effects on the body, not mainly to treat illness.
Extra cue: Some recreational drugs are legal and some are illegal.

Front: Which list contains stimulants from the revision pack examples?
Back: caffeine, cocaine and ecstasy
Extra cue: Stimulants speed up the nervous system.
Choices: caffeine, cocaine and ecstasy|alcohol, heroin and solvents|paracetamol and penicillin|water and plasma

Front: Which list contains depressants from the revision pack examples?
Back: alcohol, heroin and solvents
Extra cue: Depressants slow down the nervous system.
Choices: alcohol, heroin and solvents|caffeine, cocaine and ecstasy|paracetamol and penicillin|oxygen and glucose

Front: Which two examples are medicines rather than stimulants or depressants?
Back: paracetamol and penicillin
Extra cue: Paracetamol treats pain; penicillin is an antibiotic.
Choices: paracetamol and penicillin|caffeine and cocaine|alcohol and heroin|ecstasy and nicotine

Front: Addictive
Back: Able to make someone feel they need to keep taking a drug.
Extra cue: Addiction is one reason drug abuse can be dangerous.

Front: Give one short-term and one long-term effect that drugs can have.
Back: Short-term effects can include changed reaction time, mood, alertness or coordination; long-term abuse can damage organs or cause addiction.
Extra cue: A good answer names the drug where possible, for example alcohol can slow reactions and damage the liver if abused.

Front: Why can depressants increase accident risk?
Back: They slow nervous-system impulses and can increase reaction time.
Extra cue: Slower reactions make it harder to respond quickly.
Choices: They slow nervous-system impulses and can increase reaction time.|They make bones conduct electricity.|They neutralise stomach acid.|They make capillary walls thicker.

Front: Why must new medicines be tested before doctors use them widely?
Back: To check that they work, find a safe dose, and identify harmful side-effects.
Extra cue: Testing reduces risk before many people use the medicine.

Front: A student says: “All drugs are illegal and harmful.” What is wrong?
Back: Some drugs are medicines that can help treat illness, but drugs can also have risks and side-effects.
Extra cue: Drug means chemical that affects the body; it does not always mean illegal drug.

Front: Citric acid
Back: An acid found in citrus fruits such as lemons and oranges.
Extra cue: Lemon juice is acidic.

Front: Ethanoic acid
Back: The acid found in vinegar.
Extra cue: Vinegar is an everyday acidic liquid.

Front: Red cabbage indicator
Back: A natural indicator made from red cabbage juice that changes colour in acids and alkalis.
Extra cue: It is useful for simple school tests of pH type.

Front: Phenolphthalein
Back: An indicator that is colourless in more acidic solutions and pink in more alkaline solutions.
Extra cue: Useful in neutralisation/titration demonstrations.

Front: Methyl orange
Back: An indicator that is red in more acidic solutions and yellow in more alkaline solutions.
Extra cue: It gives different colours in acidic and alkaline solutions.

Front: Which everyday liquid is acidic because it contains ethanoic acid?
Back: vinegar
Extra cue: Ethanoic acid is the acid in vinegar.
Choices: vinegar|oven cleaner|washing powder|pure water

Front: Which everyday liquid is acidic because it contains citric acid?
Back: lemon juice
Extra cue: Citrus fruits contain citric acid.
Choices: lemon juice|toothpaste|washing powder|indigestion powder

Front: Which of these is neutral on the pH scale?
Back: pure water
Extra cue: Neutral solutions have pH 7.
Choices: pure water|stomach acid|oven cleaner|vinegar

Front: Which example is usually alkaline?
Back: toothpaste

Front: How can you make a natural indicator from red cabbage?
Back: Crush or chop red cabbage, mix it with a small amount of water, filter or decant the coloured liquid, then test it with known acids and alkalis.
Extra cue: Use known solutions first so you can compare the colour changes.

Front: How should you use an indicator to test an unknown liquid?
Back: Add a few drops of indicator to a small sample, observe the colour, and compare with known results or a pH colour chart.
Extra cue: Use small samples and wear eye protection.

Front: Which tool gives a numerical pH reading directly?
Back: pH meter
Extra cue: Universal indicator estimates pH from colour; a pH meter gives a reading.
Choices: pH meter|litmus paper|evaporating dish|ammeter

Front: What does universal indicator paper need to be compared with?
Back: a pH colour chart
Extra cue: The colour chart converts the indicator colour into an estimated pH.
Choices: a pH colour chart|a circuit symbol|a pulse rate|a tendon

Front: sulfuric acid + magnesium oxide → ?

Front: nitric acid + zinc oxide → ?
Back: zinc nitrate + water
Extra cue: Nitric acid makes nitrate salts; zinc oxide is a base.

Front: hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide → ?
Back: potassium chloride + water

Front: sulfuric acid + calcium oxide → ?
Back: calcium sulfate + water
Extra cue: Acid + base makes salt + water.

Front: nitric acid + sodium hydroxide → ?
Back: sodium nitrate + water
Extra cue: Sodium comes from sodium hydroxide; nitrate comes from nitric acid.

Front: Which salt is made from sulfuric acid and copper oxide?
Back: copper sulfate
Extra cue: Copper comes from copper oxide; sulfate comes from sulfuric acid.
Choices: copper sulfate|copper chloride|sodium sulfate|magnesium nitrate

Front: Which salt is made from hydrochloric acid and zinc oxide?
Back: zinc chloride
Extra cue: Zinc comes from zinc oxide; chloride comes from hydrochloric acid.
Choices: zinc chloride|zinc nitrate|sodium chloride|magnesium sulfate

Front: How do antacids help with indigestion?
Back: They contain a base or alkali that neutralises extra stomach acid.
Extra cue: Neutralisation makes salt and water.

Front: Why can toothpaste help protect teeth from acids?
Back: Toothpaste is mildly alkaline and helps neutralise acids in the mouth.
Extra cue: Acids in the mouth can attack teeth.

Front: Why might farmers add a base to soil?
Back: To neutralise soil that is too acidic for crops.
Extra cue: This is an everyday neutralisation example.

Front: Why are alkalis used with acidic gases from power stations?
Back: The alkali neutralises the acidic gases before they are released.
Extra cue: This reduces harm from acidic pollution.

Front: How can sulfuric acid help remove rust?
Back: It reacts with iron oxide in rust to make iron sulfate, helping remove rust from the surface.
Extra cue: This is an acid + metal oxide reaction example.

Front: A student says: “Diluting an acid makes it an alkali.” What is wrong?
Back: Diluting an acid makes it less concentrated and usually less acidic, but it does not turn it into an alkali.
Extra cue: The pH moves closer to 7 but stays below 7 unless a neutralisation reaction happens.

Front: A student says: “A concentrated acid is always the same idea as a strong acid.” What is wrong?
Back: Concentrated means a lot of acid particles in a certain volume; strong acid is a different chemistry idea. In Year 7, use more acidic/less acidic when reading pH.
Extra cue: This app now avoids using strong when it only means low pH.

Front: Physical model
Back: A model that you can touch or build to represent something.
Extra cue: Example: a water/central-heating model of a circuit.

Front: Abstract model
Back: A model that exists as an idea, drawing, equation or diagram rather than a touchable object.
Extra cue: Circuit diagrams and mental models can be abstract models.

Front: Scientific model
Back: A simplified representation used to explain or predict how something works.
Extra cue: Models are useful but they are not exactly the same as the real thing.

Front: Why is a central-heating system a useful model for an electric circuit?
Back: It helps picture flow around a loop, even though charges are too small to see directly.
Extra cue: Models help explain invisible processes, but they are never perfect copies.
Choices: It helps picture flow around a loop, even though charges are too small to see directly.|It proves electricity is actually water in wires.|It removes the need to test real circuits.|It shows that charge disappears inside bulbs.

Front: In the central-heating model of a circuit, what represents the cell or power supply?
Back: The boiler and pump.
Extra cue: They provide the push/energy, like the cell in a circuit.

Front: In the central-heating model of a circuit, what represent the wires?
Back: The pipes.
Extra cue: Pipes carry water around the heating system; wires provide the path for charges.

Front: In the central-heating model of a circuit, what represent the bulbs?
Back: The radiators.
Extra cue: Radiators transfer energy in the model, like bulbs transfer electrical energy to light and heat.

Front: Why is the central-heating model not exactly the same as an electric circuit?
Back: Water is not the same as electric charge, and the parts of the heating system do not behave exactly like circuit components.
Extra cue: A model is useful when it helps explain some features, but it always has limits.

Front: Which example is a physical model rather than an abstract model?
Back: A touchable model circuit made with pipes and a pump.
Extra cue: Physical models can be touched or built; abstract models are ideas, diagrams or simulations.
Choices: A touchable model circuit made with pipes and a pump.|The idea that voltage is like a push.|A truth table for switches.|A circuit diagram only drawn on paper.

Front: Which example is an abstract model of a circuit?
Back: A circuit diagram used to represent a real circuit.
Extra cue: A circuit diagram is not the real circuit; it represents the parts and connections.
Choices: A circuit diagram used to represent a real circuit.|A working circuit made from cells, wires and bulbs.|A plastic model of a plug.|A metal wire used in an experiment.

Front: AND circuit: switch A is open and switch B is closed. What happens to the lamp?
Back: The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed.
Extra cue: In an AND circuit, one open switch is enough to break the path.
Choices: The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed.|The lamp lights because switch B is closed.|The lamp lights dimly because one switch is closed.|The lamp becomes brighter than normal.

Front: AND circuit: switch A is closed and switch B is closed. What happens to the lamp?
Back: The lamp lights because the complete path is closed.
Extra cue: Both switches closed satisfies the AND condition.
Choices: The lamp lights because the complete path is closed.|The lamp stays off because an AND circuit never lights.|The current stops at the second switch.|Only one switch may be closed in an AND circuit.

Front: OR circuit: switch A is open and switch B is closed. What happens to the lamp?
Back: The lamp lights because one complete branch is enough.
Extra cue: In an OR circuit, either switch can complete a path.
Choices: The lamp lights because one complete branch is enough.|The lamp stays off because both switches must be closed.|The lamp lights only if switch A is closed instead.|The cell voltage becomes zero.

Front: OR circuit: switch A is open and switch B is open. What happens to the lamp?
Back: The lamp stays off because neither branch is complete.
Extra cue: OR needs at least one closed branch.
Choices: The lamp stays off because neither branch is complete.|The lamp lights because there are two branches.|The lamp flashes because current swaps branches.|The lamp lights if the wires are metal.

Front: Voltage division in series
Back: In a series circuit, the supply voltage is shared between components.
Extra cue: More components in series share the energy transfer.

Front: Voltage in parallel
Back: Components connected across the same cell in parallel get the same voltage as each other.
Extra cue: Each branch has its own path across the supply.

Front: Two identical lamps are connected in series across one cell. Which statement about voltage is best?
Back: The supply voltage is shared between the two lamps.
Extra cue: In series, voltage is divided across components.
Choices: The supply voltage is shared between the two lamps.|Each lamp gets the full supply voltage independently.|The first lamp uses all the voltage and the second gets none.|Voltage only exists in the wires, not across lamps.

Front: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across the same cell. Which statement about voltage is best?
Back: Each branch gets the same supply voltage.
Extra cue: Parallel branches are connected across the same two points.
Choices: Each branch gets the same supply voltage.|The top branch gets all the voltage.|The voltage is split equally between the branches.|The voltage becomes current in each branch.

Front: Electrical shock
Back: Injury caused when electric current passes through the body.
Extra cue: Severe shocks can stop the heart working.

Front: Electrical burn
Back: A burn caused by electricity heating body tissue or materials.
Extra cue: Electricity can cause burns and fires if used unsafely.

Front: Which set lists realistic hazards from unsafe electricity use?
Back: Electric shock, burns and fire.
Extra cue: Hazards can cause harm; safe features reduce risk.
Choices: Electric shock, burns and fire.|High current, overheating and electric shock.|Loose cable grip, damaged insulation and wet hands.|Correct fuse, insulated wire and switched-off supply.

Front: Why does using electrical equipment with wet hands increase risk?
Back: Water can lower the resistance of the path through your body, so current may pass more easily.
Extra cue: Current through the body can be dangerous.
Choices: Water can lower the resistance of the path through your body, so current may pass more easily.|Water always turns the circuit off before current flows.|Wet skin makes voltage disappear.|Water changes live wire into earth wire.

Front: Several high-current appliances are connected to one socket. What is the main danger?
Back: Too much current can overheat the wires and start a fire.
Extra cue: Overload means current is larger than the wiring or fuse rating should allow.
Choices: Too much current can overheat the wires and start a fire.|The voltage becomes shared equally between people.|The neutral wire turns into an insulator.|The appliance becomes a parallel model.

Front: Before changing a bulb or resistor in a school circuit, what should you do first?
Back: Switch off the power supply.
Extra cue: Always make the circuit safe before touching or changing components.
Choices: Switch off the power supply.|Increase the voltage to test it faster.|Hold both terminals to check current.|Remove the insulating cover from the leads.

Front: Why are cells usually used for school circuit experiments instead of mains electricity?
Back: Cells provide a much lower voltage, so the risk is lower.
Extra cue: Lower voltage does not mean zero risk, but it is safer for classroom circuits.
Choices: Cells provide a much lower voltage, so the risk is lower.|Cells have no electrical energy.|Cells cannot produce current.|Mains electricity is only dangerous in series circuits.

Front: A fault causes a very large current. What happens to the fuse?
Back: The fuse wire melts and opens the circuit.
Extra cue: Fuse rating is the largest current a fuse should carry before melting.
Choices: The fuse wire melts and opens the circuit.|The fuse wire gets thicker and carries more current.|The fuse measures voltage across the appliance.|The fuse changes live wire into neutral wire.

Front: How is a circuit breaker similar to a fuse?
Back: It cuts off the current when the current is too large.
Extra cue: Unlike a fuse, a circuit breaker can usually be reset.
Choices: It cuts off the current when the current is too large.|It increases current to protect the appliance.|It measures resistance in the earth wire.|It turns series circuits into parallel circuits.

Front: Which row gives the correct UK-style plug wire colours?
Back: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green/yellow.
Extra cue: Brown = live; blue = neutral; green/yellow = earth.
Choices: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green/yellow.|Live blue, neutral brown, earth green/yellow.|Live green/yellow, neutral blue, earth brown.|Live red, neutral black, earth blue.

Front: Two wires are made from the same material and have the same length. Which wire has higher resistance?
Back: The thinner wire.
Extra cue: Thin wires have less space for charges to flow, so resistance is higher.
Choices: The thinner wire.|The thicker wire.|They must both have zero resistance.|The wire connected to the voltmeter only.

Front: A wire is made longer, but the material and thickness stay the same. What happens to resistance?
Back: Resistance increases.
Extra cue: Longer wires usually have greater resistance.
Choices: Resistance increases.|Resistance decreases to zero.|Current becomes the unit volt.|The wire becomes a cell.

Front: Which set of factors can affect the resistance of a wire?
Back: Length, thickness and material.
Extra cue: At this level, these are the main wire factors to remember.
Choices: Length, thickness and material.|Colour, smell and shape of the plug.|Only the number of switches.|Only whether the wire is in series.

Front: Why are house lights usually wired in parallel rather than series?
Back: Parallel wiring lets each light have its own branch, so lights can be switched independently and one broken lamp does not turn all the others off.
Extra cue: This matches the revision pack idea that branches stay on when another branch breaks.

Front: How can a variable resistor control a lamp or motor?
Back: Changing resistance changes the current, which can change lamp brightness or motor speed.
Extra cue: Higher resistance usually means lower current.

Front: In the plug-safety diagram, which label shows the cable grip?

Front: In the dilution safety diagram, which label shows the safe pouring direction?
Back: C

Back: A
Extra cue: Label A points to the ruler that is dropped.
Choices: A|B|C

Front: In the ruler-drop test diagram, which label shows the catching hand?
Back: B

Front: In the ruler-drop test diagram, which label shows the measured falling distance?

Back: B
